title: 3-Read Friday #20: Wrong Answers, 100 Percent, and Task Writing
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton's 3-Read Friday #20 curates three posts on wrong answers, classroom compliance, and task design. Dan Meyer summarises research by Sarah Shi Hui Wong showing that deliberately asking students to generate and then correct a wrong answer improves recall more than simply copying a correct definition, and argues teachers should proactively request wrong answers rather than just tolerating them. Dylan Kane unpacks the popular but vague "insist on 100 percent" classroom-management advice, arguing the real skill lies in avoiding public power struggles and instead following up individually with students who opt out. Dan Draper walks through a set of maths tasks he wrote for Year 11s, cataloguing the small, unintended ways students found unplanned patterns or shortcuts across supposedly independent questions. Barton connects the three as a reminder that precision -- in how wrong answers are used, how compliance is pursued, and how questions are sequenced -- separates good technique from good-sounding slogans.
points: Dan Meyer cites Wong's finding that students who copied a definition, deliberately introduced an error, and then corrected it outperformed students who simply copied the definition correctly.

Dylan Kane reframes "100 percent" compliance advice: the risk isn't accepting less than 100 percent once, it's the slippery slope from 90 to 80 to 50 percent, and the fix is individual follow-up rather than public confrontation.

Dan Draper's task-writing retrospective catalogues four specific unintended consequences -- from students spotting a shared answer across supposedly unrelated questions to a rectangle sketched with the wrong proportions -- and how he revised each one.

Barton's throughline: all three posts turn a familiar, general-sounding piece of advice ("use wrong answers," "insist on 100 percent," "write good tasks") into something much more specific and actionable.
quotes: My motto with a multiple-choice diagnostic question is that learning does not need to stop with the correct answer.
Challenging students to explain reasons for incorrect answers, or change the question as little as possible to make wrong answers correct is so powerful.
If you accept less than 100% of students following an instruction, you risk a slippery slope.

Dan reflects on a set of practice questions he gave his students that look perfectly fine at first glance, but which have a few unintended consequences that have the potential to confuse students and hinder learning.
This hammers home the importance of careful question selection and working through tasks yourself first - something I have fallen foul of in the past.
